content:
For most Indian NGOs, the best domain is a short, easy-to-spell version of the organisation's name on **.org** or **.org.in**, registered in the name of the organisation itself (not a staff member, trustee or web developer), with the login held by at least two people inside the NGO and auto-renewal switched on. The newer **.ngo** extension is a legitimate option with an extra eligibility check, and can work well as a second domain that redirects to your main site, but few Indian donors type it from memory. What matters far more than the extension is ownership, renewal and email setup: we regularly see NGOs whose domain is registered to a volunteer who left years ago, whose website disappeared because a card expired, or whose donation receipts land in spam because the email records were never set up. Getting this right is part of any serious NGO website development project in India, and it costs very little to fix early.

This guide is for founders, programme heads and administrators of trusts, societies and Section 8 companies. It explains how to choose a name, the differences between .org, .org.in, .in and .ngo, who should own the domain, how to protect it, how to set up email on it so receipts and appeals are delivered, and what to do if your domain is currently controlled by someone else.

## Why the domain matters more for an NGO than for most businesses

For a shop, a forgotten domain renewal means a few days of lost sales. For an NGO, it can mean:

- **Donation links on old posters, pamphlets and WhatsApp forwards stop working,** often in the middle of a campaign.
- **Receipts and 80G certificates stop arriving** because email on the domain fails.
- **Donors and CSR teams lose confidence.** A domain that does not resolve, or that suddenly shows a parking page or adverts, looks like a closed or fraudulent organisation.
- **Someone else can register a lapsed domain** after the grace periods end and use your name, sometimes for scams that exploit your reputation.
- **Search visibility built over years is lost.**

The domain is also the address donors check when deciding whether a fundraising message is genuine. A consistent, recognisable domain across your website, emails, receipts and campaign links is one of the simplest trust signals you have.
## Choosing the name

### Keep it short and spellable

The name will be spoken at events, printed on banners and typed into phones by people who heard it once. Prefer:

- The organisation's name or a well-known short form, if available
- No hyphens unless unavoidable (they are hard to say out loud)
- No numbers that could be spelt either way ("4" or "four")
- No unusual spellings

If your registered name is long, such as "Shri Sai Seva Charitable Trust, Pune", consider a short form people already use, such as "saisevatrust", and register the full name as a second domain that redirects.

### Check before you commit

- **Search for the name** to see whether another organisation uses something similar. Confusion with a better-known charity or company can cause problems, including trademark disputes.
- **Check social media handles** at the same time, so your website, Instagram and Facebook can match where possible.
- **Say it aloud on a phone call.** If people need it spelt every time, choose something simpler.

### Register the obvious variations

Domains are cheap compared with the cost of confusion. Consider registering your main name on .org and .org.in (and .in if available), plus common misspellings for a large organisation, and redirect them all to one main domain. Do not build separate websites on each; one site with redirects is easier to maintain and better for search.

## The extensions compared

| Extension | Who runs it | Who can register | Notes for Indian NGOs |
|---|---|---|---|
| .org | Public Interest Registry (PIR) | Anyone; no proof of non-profit status required | Widely recognised by donors in India and abroad as a non-profit signal |
| .org.in | NIXI (.IN Registry) | Originally intended for non-profits; registrars describe it as open, with India's .IN registration and verification rules applying | Signals both "organisation" and "India"; useful for domestic donors |
| .in | NIXI (.IN Registry) | Open | Short and Indian, but carries no non-profit signal |
| .ngo | Public Interest Registry (PIR) | Organisations meeting PIR's NGO criteria; eligibility checks apply | Clear non-profit signal, but less familiar to Indian donors |
| .com | Verisign | Anyone | Recognisable, but some donors associate it with businesses |

A few points to understand:

- **.org is not verified.** Anyone can register a .org, including businesses. It is a convention, not a credential. Donors and CSR teams who check carefully will still look for your registration details, 12A/80G information and NGO Darpan ID on the site.
- **.ngo has an eligibility check.** PIR defines an NGO using a set of characteristics, including acting in the public interest, non-profit orientation, limited government influence and lawful conduct. PIR audits registrations and can cancel domains that do not meet its policy. The verification process has changed over the years (registrars report a move from document-based pre-validation to self-certification with audits), so check PIR's current policy when you register. .ngo and its sister .ong have been sold separately since 2022.
- **.IN domains now involve stricter verification.** NIXI, which runs .in and its sub-domains such as .org.in, has introduced registrant verification requirements, and registrars have been asking existing holders as well as new registrants to complete them. Make sure the organisation's correct, current details are on the registration so you can pass any checks.

Policies change, so treat this table as a starting point and confirm current rules with your registrar or the registry before you buy.

### Which should you choose?

For most Indian NGOs we suggest:

- **Main domain:** whichever of .org or .org.in you can get with a clean, short name. If you raise significant funds from abroad (with FCRA registration), .org may be marginally more familiar to overseas donors; if your donors are mostly in India, .org.in works well.
- **Secondary domains:** the other of .org/.org.in, the .in, and optionally .ngo, all redirecting to the main domain.
- **Avoid changing your main domain** once it is established unless there is a strong reason. A domain change needs a careful redirect map so search rankings, old campaign links and printed QR codes keep working.

## Who should own the domain: the most important decision

The domain should be registered in the name of the organisation, with organisation-controlled contact details, in an account the organisation controls. In practice:

### Registrant name

The "registrant" on the domain record should be the trust, society or Section 8 company, using its legal name. Not the founder personally, not a volunteer and not the web agency. If a dispute ever arises, the registrant is the legal holder.

### Account access

- Create the registrar account using an organisation email address that is not tied to one person, for example admin@ or it@ your domain, or a shared role mailbox.
- Give at least two trusted people inside the organisation access, for example the executive director and the finance or admin head.
- Turn on two-factor authentication on the registrar account.
- Store login details in a password manager or a sealed record with the trustees, so access survives staff changes.

### Your web developer's role

Your developer may need access to change DNS records. Give them a separate user login where the registrar supports it, or make the changes yourself on their instructions. Avoid letting a developer register the domain in their own account "for convenience". This is one of the most common causes of NGOs losing control of their domain when a relationship ends. Our checklist of [what to ask for when comparing vendor quotations](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-website-brief-vendor-quotation-comparison-2026) includes this as a contract point.

## Protecting the domain from lapsing

### Renewal

- Turn on **auto-renewal** at the registrar.
- Use a payment method that does not expire with one person's departure, ideally an organisation card or prepaid account balance, and update it when cards are replaced.
- Renew for **several years at once** where the registrar allows it. It costs little and removes risk.
- Put the expiry date in the organisation's compliance calendar alongside 12A/80G and FCRA dates, with reminders 60 and 30 days before.

### Registrar lock and privacy

- Keep **transfer lock** (sometimes called registrar lock) on, so the domain cannot be moved to another registrar without deliberate action.
- Use the registrar's privacy option for personal contact details if it is offered for your extension, but make sure the organisation remains the registrant and that renewal notices reach a monitored inbox.

### DNS and SSL

Domain registration, DNS hosting and SSL certificates are related but separate. Your site can go down because the domain expired, because DNS was misconfigured, or because the SSL certificate was not renewed. Our guide to [domain, DNS and SSL renewals](/blog/web-development-company-pune-domain-dns-ssl-renewal-website-downtime-2026) explains each and how to monitor them.

## Email on your domain: receipts that actually arrive

Using your domain for email (for example donations@ or info@ yourngo.org) looks more trustworthy than a free webmail address, and donors are more likely to recognise and open messages from it. But email on a custom domain only works reliably if it is set up properly.

### Choose a proper email service

Use a business email service rather than relying on the email that comes bundled with cheap shared hosting. Several major providers offer discounted or donated plans for eligible non-profits; check their current non-profit programmes and eligibility rules for Indian organisations.

### Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC

These three DNS records tell receiving mail servers that messages claiming to come from your domain are genuine. Without them, donation receipts, 80G certificates and appeals are more likely to land in spam or be rejected. Google and Yahoo tightened their requirements for bulk senders in 2024, including authentication and an easy unsubscribe for marketing mail. Your website, donation platform, CRM and email marketing tool may all send mail on your behalf, so each needs to be included in your SPF and signed with DKIM. Our guide to [SPF, DKIM and DMARC for website emails](/blog/web-development-company-pune-email-deliverability-spf-dkim-dmarc-2026) walks through the setup.

### Use role addresses

Create addresses for roles rather than people: donations@, receipts@, csr@, volunteer@, info@. When staff change, the address stays and is simply reassigned. Donors who saved your receipts address can still reach you.

### Keep donor communications consistent

Send receipts, appeals and newsletters from your domain, not from a staff member's personal account. It is more professional, it is easier to authenticate, and it supports your data protection obligations by keeping donor communications inside systems the organisation controls.

## What to do if someone else controls your domain

This situation is common. A founder's relative registered it years ago, a former employee holds the login, or a previous web agency registered it in its own account. Steps:

1. **Find out who the registrar is.** A WHOIS or RDAP lookup on the domain shows the registrar and expiry date, even when contact details are hidden.
2. **Ask the current holder, in writing, to transfer it.** Most people cooperate when asked politely. For a former agency, check the contract; many agreements state that the client owns the domain.
3. **Use the registrar's transfer process.** The holder unlocks the domain and provides an authorisation (EPP) code; you initiate the transfer to an account the organisation controls. Alternatively, some registrars allow an internal change of account holder.
4. **Update the registrant details** to the organisation's legal name and role contacts.
5. **If the holder refuses or cannot be found,** speak to the registrar about their dispute process and take legal advice. Domain disputes over names that match an organisation's established name can be handled through formal dispute resolution processes, but these take time and money, so prevention is far cheaper.

Do not let the domain lapse in the hope of re-registering it; someone else may register it first.

## A checklist for your NGO's domain

- [ ] Main domain is short, spellable and matches the organisation name or a well-known short form
- [ ] Registrant is the organisation's legal name, not an individual or agency
- [ ] Registrar account uses a role email and is accessible to at least two people in the organisation
- [ ] Two-factor authentication is on
- [ ] Auto-renewal is on, with a payment method that will not lapse
- [ ] Domain is renewed several years ahead and the expiry date is in the compliance calendar
- [ ] Transfer lock is on
- [ ] Secondary domains (.org, .org.in, .in, optionally .ngo) redirect to the main domain
- [ ] Business email set up on the domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] Receipts, appeals and newsletters send from role addresses on the domain
- [ ] SSL certificate auto-renews and is monitored
- [ ] Your web developer has the access they need, but not ownership

## How Govindani handles domains on NGO projects

Having engineered more than 500 non-profit websites, we check domain ownership at the start of every NGO project, and we set clients up so the organisation owns its domain, holds the registrar login and has email authentication in place before launch, including for receipts sent from donation platforms such as our Give Setu system. If you are planning a new NGO website, moving to a new domain, or unsure who controls your current one, see our [NGO website development service](/pages/ngopage/), our [website creation service](/services/website-creation), or [contact us](/contact-us) and call 092019 58274.

## Frequently asked questions

### Should an NGO use .org or .org.in?
Either works. .org is recognised worldwide as a non-profit convention, though anyone can register one. .org.in signals an Indian organisation and suits NGOs whose donors are mainly in India. Many NGOs register both and redirect one to the other.

### Can any organisation register a .ngo domain?
No. .ngo is run by Public Interest Registry, which sets eligibility criteria for non-governmental organisations, such as acting in the public interest and being non-profit, and audits registrations. Check PIR's current verification process before registering.

### Who should own our NGO's domain name?
The organisation itself. The registrant should be the trust, society or Section 8 company's legal name, and the registrar account should use an organisation email with at least two people inside the NGO holding access. Your web developer should not be the owner.

### Why are our donation receipts going to spam?
Usually because the domain sending them is not authenticated. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for every service that sends email for you, including your website, donation platform and email tool, and send from a proper business email service rather than basic shared hosting mail.

### What happens if our NGO's domain expires?
The website and email on it stop working, often after a short grace period, and old donation links break. If it is not renewed within the registry's redemption period, it can be released and registered by someone else. Turn on auto-renewal and renew several years ahead.

Sources:
- [Public Interest Registry: .NGO and .ONG policy](https://pir.org/our-impact/ngo-ong-policy/)
- [.IN Registry (NIXI): Registry advisory, July 2025](https://registry.in/registry-advisory-2025_07_29)
- [IANA: Redelegation of the .IN domain to NIXI](https://www.iana.org/reports/2009/in-report-27nov2009.html)
- [Google Workspace Admin Help: Email sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126)
- [ICANN: Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/help/dndr/udrp-en)

*About the author: written by the Govindani Infotech NGO technology team in Pune, who have engineered more than 500 non-profit websites and the Give Setu donation platform, and who handle domain, DNS and email setup for NGO clients across India.*
